check.title: Is this really us?
check.intro: Fraudsters sometimes pretend to be wealth managers. This is how to tell a real call or email from us.
never: Ask you to move money to a new or "safe" account.
Tell you about a change to our bank details by email or text.
Ask for a password, a PIN or a one-time code.
Rush you to decide on the same call.
check.callback: If anything feels wrong, hang up and call us back on the number above, from a different phone if you can. We will never mind you checking.

items.title: Selling your business: what to sort out in the year before
items.summary: The months before a sale decide much of what follows it. A short list of what owners tend to settle first, and who usually helps with each.
body: Most of the work that shapes life after a sale happens before it. Owners who start a year ahead usually have more choices than those who start at heads of terms.

The first questions are rarely about investments. Who in the family owns shares, and should that change before a sale? What will the business pay you between now and completion? Where will the proceeds sit on the day they arrive?

Your solicitor and accountant lead on the structure of the sale itself. Our part is the plan for you and your family around it: what you will need, what you would like to do, and what the money should be ready for.
items.author: Tom Ashworth

items.title: Gifts from surplus income: how families use them
items.summary: Regular gifts made out of income can sit outside inheritance tax if they follow the rules. What the rules look for, and why records matter.
body: UK inheritance tax treats some gifts as exempt when they are made regularly out of income, form a pattern, and leave the giver's usual standard of living unchanged. Gifts made out of capital don't count.

Families use it to pay school fees for grandchildren, to fund a child's pension, or to support a relative. Executors may later need to show that each gift met the rules, so a simple record kept each year makes that much easier.
Whether it suits you depends on your income, your spending and your wider plans. It is worth discussing with us and your solicitor before you start.
items.author: Priya Nair

items.title: Your first UK tax year: the questions to ask early
items.summary: Arriving in the UK changes how your income and gains are taxed. The questions worth asking before you arrive, not after.
body: The UK tax year runs from 6 April to 5 April. Whether you are UK resident in a given year is decided by the statutory residence test, which looks at the days you spend here and your ties to the UK.

Since April 2025, new arrivals are taxed under rules based on residence rather than domicile. How your existing investments, pensions and property abroad are treated can depend on when you arrive and what you do in the months before.
We work alongside tax advisers in the UK and abroad, so that the plan for your money and the plan for your tax are made together.
items.author: James Okafor

items.title: What our investment committee is watching this quarter
items.summary: The questions our investment committee is asking this autumn, and how we think about them for families investing for the long term.
body: Each quarter our investment committee reviews the world our clients' portfolios live in: interest rates, inflation, company earnings and the risks that sit outside the numbers.
We don't try to predict the next quarter. We ask whether each portfolio still fits the plan it was built for, and whether anything has changed that should change it.
If you would like to talk about your own portfolio, your adviser will go through it with you.
items.author: James Okafor

items.title: Talking to children about the family's wealth
items.summary: When and how families start the conversation about wealth with the next generation, and what tends to help.
body: Many families find that talking about money early makes later decisions easier for everyone. The right moment differs from family to family.
Some start with how the family's wealth was made and what it is for. Others bring older children into a yearly review, or into conversations about giving.
We are happy to join those conversations, or to meet the next generation on their own.
items.author: Priya Nair

items.title: Leaving a gift to charity in your will
items.summary: A gift in a will can support causes that matter to you. What to think about, and who to involve.
body: Many families want part of their estate to support a charity or cause. A gift in a will is one way to do it; giving during your lifetime, or through a charitable trust or donor-advised fund, are others.
Gifts to UK charities can also affect how much inheritance tax an estate pays. Your solicitor will draft the wording; we can help you think about how the gift fits with the rest of your plans.
items.author: Harriet Lyall
